purpose: Private editorial review candidates for a source-grounded Aerospace Folktales journey. This file is not a public association manifest.
research_limits: A named reading, ownership, date, subject similarity, or shelf placement does not by itself establish influence on Aerospace Folktales.
The oral-history matches for One-dimensional man, Galileo, and Suburbia are title-level; the sources do not identify the surviving Clark physical copies.
The Effects of Nuclear Weapons is proposed as a documented object in the work, not as an inspirational book. A Clark librarian must confirm the copy-identity claim before publication.
No Allan Sekula artwork image is included. The cited Generali, Getty, and Clark sources do not provide an open license for the work photographs.
Approval in the local review utility would still have publication_effect none; a separate editorial commit is required to publish any association.

candidates.temporal_basis: Sekula dates the reading to summer 1969 while he worked near Lockheed; the target work is dated 1973 and the Getty finding aid dates initial notes to 1972.
candidates.proposed_reasoning: Sekula states in oral history that he read One Dimensional Man at a picnic table during his 1969 Burbank chemical-plant job, in a passage about industrial corruption and his disillusionment with science. This documents a relevant pre-project reading context, but it does not establish that the surviving Clark copy was the copy read or that the book influenced Aerospace Folktales.
candidates.inference_limit: Contextual only: the source names the reading and industrial setting but never connects this title to the conception or production of Aerospace Folktales.

candidates.temporal_basis: The manual is dated 1957; Clark and Edwards identify it as a photographed subject in the 1973 work.
candidates.proposed_reasoning: Clark librarian Susan Roeper identifies Ignace Sekula's annotated 1957 copy of The Effects of Nuclear Weapons and states that it was featured as a subject in Aerospace Folktales. Steve Edwards independently describes three page spreads from the title within the work. This supports a direct object-in-work relation; it does not show that the manual inspired the project, and the surviving Clark-copy identity must be confirmed by a librarian before publication.
candidates.inference_limit: Documented object in the work, not documented inspiration. OSTI supplies an exact-year digital edition surrogate only and cannot establish the Clark copy's cover, dimensions, annotations, texture, or side profile.

candidates.temporal_basis: Aerospace Folktales is dated 1973; the Ehrenreich essays appeared in 1977 and were reprinted in this 1979 collection; Edwards says the original work predates them and that a later version was revised after their appearance.
candidates.proposed_reasoning: Steve Edwards documents Sekula's ownership of Between Labor and Capital, identifies its reprinted essays as part of the later professional-managerial-class debate, and argues that the final version of Aerospace Folktales was revised after those essays appeared. The source supports a post-project conceptual dialogue candidate, not a claim about the work's original conception or proof that this physical copy was used in a revision.
candidates.inference_limit: Scholarly post-project interpretation only: the 1979 book cannot be preliminary inspiration for a 1973 work, and the source does not document the Clark copy inside a specific revision file.
